statement: Among 116 adults in Australia who had used ecstasy at least once, surveyed in 2004 through the researchers' acquaintances and their networks and through an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter (Allott & Redman, 2006; 51 in 100 women, mean age 26.5), every respondent reported at least one thing they did to avoid ecstasy's negative side effects, chosen from a list: most often drinking water (96 in 100), limiting the amount of ecstasy (71 in 100), taking breaks or chilling out (62 in 100), a healthy lifestyle (60 in 100) and vitamins or natural products (53 in 100); 30 in 100 took other illegal drugs and 16 in 100 prescription medicines for this. To avoid the comedown in the days after, 4 in 100 had no strategy, and to avoid brain damage, 18 in 100 had none. 41 in 100 had taken pharmaceuticals or natural products before ecstasy ('preloading') and 47 in 100 after it ('postloading'): among those who listed them, half took multivitamins and 41 in 100 took 5-HTP (a building block of serotonin) before, followed by magnesium and fruit or juice, and 46 in 100 took 5-HTP and 44 in 100 multivitamins after; among those who gave reasons, 46 in 100 did it to ease the comedown and 33 in 100 to reduce brain damage. About 39 in 100 had ever tested their pills (61 in 100 never had; editors' calculation), and 53 in 100 had changed how they used ecstasy because of something they disliked about it, most of them by using it less often. Every respondent had also used at least one other substance with ecstasy, most often alcohol (91 in 100 before and 81 in 100 during use) and amphetamines (60 in 100 before and 66 in 100 during). Preloading and postloading were more common among respondents who had used ecstasy more than 50 times (preloading 55 against 30 in 100), among about 30 tests without correction. These figures describe one self-selected sample, not how common the practices are: respondents found through harm-reduction websites may be more interested in harm reduction, the response rate is unknown, the questionnaire was not validated, and how often each strategy was used was not asked. Whether any of these practices lowers harm was not studied: the authors note that the evidence that preloading protects comes only from studies in rodents given injected pre-treatments, and that taking 5-HTP, SSRI antidepressants or St John's wort with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome, which this survey did not examine. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a 2004 survey of 116 people in Australia who had used ecstasy, almost all said they drank water to avoid side effects, and most said they limited how much they took or took breaks. About 4 in 10 had taken vitamins, 5-HTP or other products before ecstasy, and about half afterwards, mostly to ease the comedown; about 4 in 10 had ever tested their pills. Many were found through harm-reduction websites, so this is not how common these habits are. Whether any of them lowers harm was not studied, and the authors warn that 5-HTP and some antidepressants taken with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive survey starts low; rated down for risk of bias (a self-selected sample likely to over-represent interest in harm reduction) and indirectness: very low. The claim gives what this sample reported, not population prevalence, and says nothing about whether any practice works, which the paper did not study. Section 7, findings only, held for the senior author: products are named as respondents reported them, with the authors' caution about serotonin syndrome, and no amounts or timings are given. One reason respondents gave for preloading, to increase the effects of ecstasy (21.8%), is left out under decision p-before-during-after (nothing on making a drug's effects stronger). The paper calls itself the first study of these practices, but its own introduction describes an earlier UK survey (Akram & Galt, 1999), not read. Later surveys of preloading (Copeland et al., 2006; Kelly, 2009) and the rat studies behind it (Sprague et al., 1994) are on the reading list and were not read. Status single study.

statement: In college students and young adults, evidence is insufficient to say whether protective behavioural strategies (things people do just before, during or after drinking to limit their drinking or its harms, such as keeping track of drinks, pacing or alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, eating, or using a designated driver) lower drinking or alcohol-related problems. In a meta-analysis of 15 randomized trials published from 2007 to 2023 (Van Nhat et al., 2026; 13 at US universities, nearly all with undergraduates aged 18 to 24), interventions that taught or prompted bundles of these strategies, mostly brief and digital and often combined with other components, compared with assessment only, education or other interventions, did not detectably change how much people said they drank (standardized difference g −0.05, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.02; 9 trials), reduced how often they said they drank by a very small amount (g −0.09, −0.17 to −0.02; 6 trials) and possibly reduced alcohol-related problems by a very small amount (g −0.07, −0.14 to 0.0007; 7 trials; −0.10, −0.19 to −0.01, after removing the largest trial, a step not described as planned); by convention a standardized difference of 0.2 counts as small. No trial tested any single strategy on its own, so the effect of eating, pacing or any other one strategy is not known; the effect on reported strategy use varied widely between trials (I² 98%) and was clear only after one 45-person pilot was removed (g 0.23, 0.07 to 0.40); 14 of the 15 trials had some concerns or a high risk of bias, all outcomes were self-reported and attrition reached 88 to 95 in 100 in one trial; whether strategy use carried the effect was tested in 6 trials, with indirect effects through it in 3 or 4 (the paper's text and tables differ). Larger effects at follow-ups of more than 3 months, and when strategies were one part of a multi-component intervention, were not tested against the other subgroups, and three of the four multi-component trials also gave personalized feedback on how others drink, so those effects cannot be credited to the strategies. Outside trials, as described second-hand in a single-author narrative review of 62 published studies found up to February 2013, which pooled no data (Pearson, 2013), students nearly always reported their strategies, drinking and problems themselves on questionnaires (at least 11 different ones), usually at one sitting and often for no stated period, so most links are associations reported by the same people, not predictions; the author estimates, without showing how, that 80% of the studies gave only cross-sectional data. By the author's account, nearly every study found that students who reported using more strategies also reported drinking less or having fewer problems, mostly as correlations whose sizes the review does not give; with one questionnaire, the link was negative when students rated how often they used strategies when they drank, but positive when they counted how many times they used them, a count that also rises with how often they drink (three studies by the author's team). In three studies, students reporting more strategies showed a weaker link between how much they drank and their problems. Over time the evidence was mixed: in a sample followed for a year after a peer intervention that showed no significant effect, correlations with later drinking were about as strong as those at the same time and changes in some kinds of strategy use went with less drinking or fewer problems, but correlations with later problems were weaker (3 of 9 not significant); in another study, strategy use rose after a brief intervention but the rise did not go with changes in drinking; and in women, strategy use was unrelated to drinking or problems at the same time point but went with fewer problems 4 months later. In two studies of day-by-day reports (a 15-day diary of 40 students, and a 7-day recall at one sitting around the 21st birthday), strategies about the way people drank went with less drinking on the days they were used, but people drank more on days they used limiting or stopping strategies, and drank more and had more problems on days with a designated driver or going home with a friend, which the author suggests reflects these strategies being planned for nights of heavy drinking. Students told to use more strategies reported using more but did not drink less (one experiment, Sugarman and Carey, 2009, which is also one of the meta-analysis's trials). In three trials of brief alcohol interventions, a rise in reported strategy use statistically mediated the interventions' effect on drinking or problems (one of them, Larimer et al., 2007, is also in the meta-analysis); in three others, the interventions did not change strategy use; none mainly targeted strategies. The author calls the trial and follow-up evidence mixed but ends by calling strategy use a promising way to reduce drinking and its harms. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.
plain: In 15 trials, mostly with US college students, teaching bundles of safety habits for drinking made very little difference: students drank very slightly less often, but the amount they drank did not clearly change, and no trial tested any one habit on its own. In surveys, students who said they used more safety habits also said they drank less, but most asked about both at the same time, and day by day students drank more on days they had a designated driver or went home with a friend, which the 2013 review's author thinks happens because these are planned for nights of heavy drinking. So whether the habits themselves lower drinking or harm is not known.
population: College students and young adults: 15 randomized trials (2007 to 2023), 13 at US universities, one at a Swedish university and one Australian pilot, mostly undergraduates aged 18 to 24 (15,714 randomized and 6,587 analysed, editors' calculation); and college students in 62 published quantitative studies found up to February 2013 (some samples appear in more than one study; countries not reported in the review), including incoming students, athletes, women and students sent to alcohol programmes, as summarized by one narrative review
exposure: Protective behavioural strategies taught or prompted in randomized trials, as bundles (limiting or stopping drinking, manner of drinking such as pacing, harm reduction such as a designated driver), alone or within multi-component interventions, mostly brief and digital; and self-reported use of strategies in observational studies, measured with at least 11 questionnaires in many versions (most often the Protective Behavioral Strategies Survey): strategies used just before, during or after drinking, such as setting a limit or leaving at a set time, alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, drinking water, eating, avoiding drinking games or mixing types of alcohol, keeping track of drinks, using a designated driver or going home with a friend; 13 of the 62 studies also counted avoiding drinking altogether
comparator: In trials: assessment only, no intervention, education or other active or attention controls, or the same intervention without a strategies booster; in observational studies: students reporting fewer strategies (between people, mostly cross-sectional), days without a given strategy (within people, two studies), control groups in trials of brief interventions, where strategy use was a measured mediator, not what was randomized, and no instruction to use strategies (one experiment)
outcome: Self-reported alcohol use (quantity, frequency, heavy drinking, estimated blood alcohol), alcohol-related problems and reported strategy use
magnitude: Van Nhat et al. (2026), random effects, Hedges' g at the longest follow-up (3 days to 12 months): quantity −0.05 (95% CI −0.13 to 0.02), 9 trials, I² 22.0%, prediction interval −0.18 to 0.07; frequency −0.09 (−0.17 to −0.02), 6 trials, I² 11.85%, prediction interval −0.19 to 0.001; problems −0.07 (−0.14 to 0.0007), p = 0.052, 7 trials, I² 0%, and −0.10 (−0.19 to −0.01) without Larimer et al. (2007); reported strategy use 0.58 (−0.21 to 1.37), 6 trials, I² 97.8%, prediction interval −1.47 to 2.63, and 0.23 (0.07 to 0.40), I² 49.9%, without O'Donnell et al. (2019). Subgroups, without between-subgroup tests (intervals only in supplements): follow-up over 3 months, quantity −0.12 and frequency −0.13; strategies as an adjunct, quantity −0.10 and frequency −0.13; as a core or primary component, no significant effect on quantity. Risk of bias: 1 trial low, 10 some concerns, 4 high (Fig. 2). Mediation through strategy use in 3 or 4 of 6 trials. Pearson (2013): no pooled estimate; the review gives sizes for almost none of the strategy–outcome links. As described: nearly every study found that students reporting more strategies reported drinking less and/or fewer problems; with one questionnaire, correlations with drinking were negative on a how-often-when-drinking scale and positive on a scale counting the number of times strategies were used, which also counts drinking occasions (3 studies); a weaker drinking–problems link in 3 studies; in one sample followed for 12 months, prospective correlations with drinking similar to same-time ones, change in some kinds of strategy use predicting less drinking or fewer problems, and 3 of 9 prospective correlations with problems not significant; day by day (2 studies, one a 15-day diary of 40 students): less drinking on days with manner-of-drinking strategies, more on days with limiting or stopping strategies, more drinking and more problems on days with serious harm reduction strategies; mediation of intervention effects in 3 trials, no change in strategy use in 3 trials; no fall in drinking after an instruction to use more strategies (1 experiment). Studies with only cross-sectional data: 80% by the author's estimate (not derived; editors' rough count from the review's appendix, about 74% to 77%).

risk_of_bias.note: Trials (card sc_van_nhat_2026): 14 of 15 at some concerns or high risk of bias by the review's RoB 2 figure, mainly from deviations from the intended interventions and missing outcome data; every outcome self-reported; attrition up to 95%; no sensitivity analysis by risk of bias. inconsistency.note: The trial estimates for drinking and problems agree (I² 0% to 22%). The observational findings point different ways by strategy and design (less drinking between people, more on days with some strategies), which the status 'mixed' records; the very heterogeneous effect on reported strategy use (I² 98%) is not a drinking outcome. Not rated down, because the graded finding rests on the trials.

indirectness.note: No trial isolated a single strategy: strategies were taught in bundles, often with personalized normative feedback, against a mix of controls, so the effect of the strategies themselves, or of strategies people choose on their own, is not measured; almost all participants were young US university students.

imprecision.note: The intervals for quantity, frequency and problems are narrow and exclude more than a small effect (none goes beyond −0.19); the problems estimate reaches no difference.

publication_bias.note: No funnel asymmetry in any pool, though with 6 to 9 trials the tests have little power; English-language peer-reviewed reports only, without trial registries or grey literature. Not rated down.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; rated down for risk of bias (14 of 15 trials at some concerns or high risk, self-reported outcomes) and indirectness (bundles taught with other components, not single strategies; US students), giving low for what the trials show: teaching bundles of strategies changed reported drinking very little. The relation stays insufficient evidence for the claim's question, whether the strategies themselves lower drinking or harms: no trial tested any single strategy, the bundles' effects are very small and partly attributable to other components, and the observational associations, which by themselves would be very low (narrative review only), point different ways by design. The meta-analysis is AMSTAR 2 low confidence (provisional: its list of excluded studies is in an appendix not read), searched English-language peer-reviewed reports only, and its abstract leads with estimates made after dropping a trial; its PRISMA counts do not add up (564 records by database against 514 printed). Counted once: Larimer et al. (2007) and Sugarman and Carey (2009), described in the 2013 review, are among the meta-analysis's trials. Status mixed: the observational findings differ in direction by strategy and design, with only the review author's untested explanation, while the trials show very small or no effects. The claim no longer rests only on a narrative review.

statement: In people who use drugs in North America who tested their drugs (or, in some studies, their urine) with fentanyl test strips, on their own without supervision or with staff at a supervised injection site (2016 to 2023), a result showing fentanyl was followed, by people's own account or by intentions they stated to staff, by a safer way of using in a minority to a majority of cases, most often using less, going slower or using with someone else around, and seldom by throwing the drug away; in each primary study read, fewer than half said they used, or would use, less; in the largest, most results were followed by using the same amount, and there a result not showing fentanyl was followed more often than one showing it by reports of using more; no study read observed what people then took. In a Rhode Island research pilot (2017), of 31 young adults who said a strip had shown fentanyl, 45 in 100 said they then used smaller amounts, 42 went slower, 39 used with someone else around, 36 tried a small amount first (a 'tester'), 10 threw the drugs out, 10 sold them and 7 gave them away; these answers were given at least two weeks later, the results were not checked, and how many used the drugs as usual was not reported. At a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016 to 2017), staff recorded an intention to use less after 142 of 391 checks before use that showed fentanyl (36 in 100), against 7 of 122 that did not (6 in 100), and an intention to throw the drug away after 50 of 436 (11 in 100) against 10 of 134 (7 in 100); what people then did was not recorded. In a British Columbia take-home programme (2019), asked a standard question (not about their own results) about what they did when a strip showed fentanyl, 217 of 336 answers (65 in 100) described no change, 86 (26 in 100) at least one safer change and 6 (2 in 100) a riskier one (using alone, or using more or faster). In a Baltimore pilot (2018 to 2019), women who sell or trade sex and use opioids were given five strips with training, counselling and naloxone; on average 56 days later, of 48 who answered about a result showing fentanyl, 33 (69 in 100) named at least one safer action, most often using a smaller amount (15, 31 in 100) or going slower when injecting (10, 21 in 100), while 30 (63 in 100) used the tested drugs, several because of withdrawal, 3 threw the drugs out, 3 sold them and none stopped using drugs; of 24 who answered about a result not showing fentanyl, 21 used their drugs as intended (Park et al., 2020). In a cohort of 541 clients of harm-reduction programmes in Kentucky, New York and Ohio who tested at least once over four weeks in 2023 and reported each week what they had done because of each result (Gelberg et al., 2025), the modelled probabilities after a result showing fentanyl, against one not showing it, were, for the amount used, the same 85 against 75 in 100, less or none 9 against 2 in 100, and more 6 against 23 in 100; and, for other actions, taking turns with someone 24 against 19 in 100, using near someone with naloxone 23 against 15 in 100, a smaller test amount first 12 against 10 in 100, and throwing the drugs away or not using them 1 to 2 in 100 after either result. The cohort's abstract calls the contrast a four-fold reduction in the amount used, but it is an odds ratio for reporting less rather than the same or more, not a measured fall in amount; results and behaviour were self-reported and not checked, and the 541 analysed were those of 1,156 enrolled who completed the surveys, used drugs and tested. A scoping review relays a median of 55 in 100 (23 to 75 in 100, seven studies) reporting some safer change, but its supplementary table shows that the top value counts changes after each result showing fentanyl rather than people and that another is the British Columbia programme's 26 in 100 answers, counted once here; the review also relays people using as usual because of withdrawal, tolerance, doubt about the result or wanting fentanyl; the evidence is mostly intentions or self-reports (one review counts 22 of its 31 behaviour studies as measuring intentions), with no comparison of people given strips with people not given them; both reviews include the Rhode Island and Vancouver studies, and the scoping review the Baltimore pilot, outside its median. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When a strip showed fentanyl, some people said they used less, went slower, used with someone else nearby or tried a small amount first, but in each study fewer than half said they used, or would use, less. Few said they threw the drug away. In the largest study, most results were followed by using the same amount, and after a result without fentanyl people more often said they used more (23 in 100, against 6 in 100 after a result with fentanyl). All of this is what people said or planned: no study watched what they actually did, and no study compared people given strips with people not given them.

statement: In people who use drugs in contact with harm-reduction services in North America, using fentanyl test strips compared with not using them: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it changes the risk of overdose. The only study read that compared the two groups followed 732 clients of strip-distributing harm-reduction sites in Kentucky, New York and Ohio for four weeks in 2023: after allowing for state, age, race, ethnicity, sex and the drugs used each day, and also for strip use and risk-reduction behaviours reported during the four weeks, which may carry part of any difference strips make, the modelled risk of a self-reported overdose that people survived (passing out and needing to be revived) was about 2 in 100 days of drug use in both groups (0.02 a day; risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.70 to 2.06, compatible with 30% fewer overdoses or twice as many); before that adjustment it was twice as high in the people who used strips (risk ratio 2.06, 1.09 to 3.89), who more often injected and used fentanyl; deaths could not be counted. A before-and-after pilot in Baltimore (2018 to 2019; Park et al., 2020), whose main planned outcome was overdose, gave five strips with training, counselling and naloxone to 103 women who sell or trade sex and use opioids: of the 68 followed up (66 in 100, on average 56 days later), 6 reported an overdose they survived (passing out) in the month before the start and 1 in the month before follow-up, a change that was not statistically significant and is not reported in the paper's abstract; there was no comparison group, the counselling addressed overdose risks, and the counts fell both in the 11 women who used no strip (2 to 0) and in the 57 who used at least one (4 to 1, by the editors' subtraction), which the paper reports separately without comparing them. A scoping review of 91 articles to March 2023 found only two that reported overdose outcomes, neither comparing people who tested with people who did not: at a supervised injection site most checks came after use (113 of the 120 overdoses were recorded with checks made after use, and a check may have been prompted by the overdose), so its lower odds of overdose among people who said they would use less (crude odds ratio 0.41) cannot show an effect; and after a vending machine began giving out strips with naloxone, county overdose deaths fell by about 10% while the state's rose by about 5%, with no control area. A systematic review of drug checking to 2019 found no other study linking testing with overdose. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In the one study that compared people who used test strips with people who did not, over four weeks, overdoses that people survived were about as common in both groups once other differences were allowed for, but the result is too uncertain to rule out either fewer or more overdoses. That comparison also allowed for the safety steps people took during the study, which could hide a difference. Deaths could not be counted. In a small Baltimore study of women given strips, 6 reported an overdose in the month before and 1 in the month before the last visit, but there was no comparison group, and the women who used no strips also had fewer. No study read could show whether strips prevent overdoses or deaths.
population: People who use drugs in contact with harm-reduction services in North America: 732 clients of 14 strip-distributing organizations in Kentucky, New York and Ohio (2023); 68 of 103 women who sell or trade sex and use opioids, followed up in a Baltimore pilot (2018–19); studies in a scoping review (to March 2023) and a systematic review of drug checking services (to October 2019)
exposure: Self-reported use of fentanyl test strips in the 30 days before baseline (cohort); strip checks at a supervised injection site, and a vending machine that dispensed strips (as relayed by the reviews); five strips with training, counselling and naloxone given to every woman (Baltimore pilot)
comparator: People at the same sites who reported no strip use (cohort); no comparison group in the two studies the scoping review describes or in the Baltimore pilot (the same women before and after)
outcome: Self-reported nonfatal overdose over four weeks (cohort); overdoses recorded by nurses with checks, and county overdose deaths and emergency visits (as relayed by the scoping review); self-reported nonfatal overdose in the month before the start and before follow-up (Baltimore pilot)
magnitude: Vickers-Smith 2025: mean daily risk 0.02 (0.01–0.03) in both groups; adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70–2.06; n = 677), from a model that also included the number of times strips were used and the risk-reduction score during follow-up (Table 3, note g); unadjusted RR 2.06 (1.09–3.89; n = 710); the association was modified by age in adjusted analyses (P = .02) but not in unadjusted ones: in the adjusted model the strip group's modelled risk was higher than the comparison group's in younger and lower in older participants, with 95% bands that overlap at every age (eFigure 5), and age was one of seven modifiers tested for this outcome and the only one reported (eMethods). Karamouzian 2018 (card): 113 of 120 overdoses recorded with checks made after use; crude OR 0.41 (0.18–0.89) for intended dose reduction pools checks made before and after use and is not an effect. risk_of_bias.note: Cohort: ROBINS-I serious (people chose to use strips; confounding by risk, with the crude ratio of 2.06 falling to 1.20 after an adjustment that left out injecting and earlier overdose but included strip use and risk-reduction behaviours during follow-up, which may hide part of any effect; 37 in 100 of those enrolled not analysed; self-reported outcomes). The two studies relayed by the review: no comparison of people who tested with people who did not, and checks that often followed the overdose. The Baltimore pilot: ROBINS-I critical (no comparison group; strips given with counselling and naloxone; 34 in 100 lost to follow-up; self-reports to study staff).

indirectness.note: Self-reported nonfatal overdose over four weeks in people already using strips at strip-distributing services; fatal overdose not measured; North American fentanyl market.

imprecision.note: The adjusted interval (0.70 to 2.06) includes a 30% reduction and a doubling, and overdoses were rare (mean daily risk 0.02). The Baltimore counts are 6 and 1.

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; risk of bias and indirectness take one level each and imprecision two: very low. 'No detectable effect' would need an interval that excludes meaningful effects (METHODS §6.3), which this one does not, and the adjustment for behaviours during follow-up may also pull the estimate towards no difference, so the claim says the evidence is insufficient. Karamouzian et al.'s odds ratio of 0.41 is reported only to say why it cannot be read as an effect (card sc_karamouzian_2018, reporting issues); Karamouzian et al. is inside both reviews (the scoping review's reference 69, by its Appendix 1; card sc_kutscher_2024) and is counted once. Status single study: only one study compared people who used strips with people who did not. The Baltimore pilot (Park et al., 2020; card sc_park_2020) adds before-and-after counts (6 to 1 women) that cannot show an effect: no comparison group, strips given with counselling and naloxone, and a fall in women who used no strip as well; it reports the two groups separately without comparing them, so the status stays single study. Its overdose result, the study's main planned outcome, is not in its abstract, and the scoping review, which includes the pilot (its reference 80) among behaviour studies, did not count it among its two articles with overdose outcomes. Gelberg et al. (2025) analysed the same Stay Safe cohort as Vickers-Smith et al. for strip results and reports no overdose outcome, so it adds no comparison and is not cited here.

statement: In people who use benzodiazepines (prescribed, diverted, counterfeit or novel 'designer' benzodiazepines; most of the sources also involved opioids or stimulants), evidence is insufficient to say whether any harm reduction service or policy lowers harm. As described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources found up to July 2025, which mapped them without appraising them (Morrison et al., 2025), the approaches studied were drug checking (11 sources), prescribed benzodiazepines as treatment or safer supply (5), policies on scheduling, prescribing and surveillance (9) and approaches for particular groups (10); by the designs listed in the review's table, 17 were quantitative pilot, retrospective, cross-sectional or similar studies, 9 qualitative, 4 mixed-methods, 4 reviews and 1 a policy analysis, and none was a randomized trial. About half of the drug-checking sources (5 or 6 of 11 by the review's table, editors' count) tested how well drug-checking methods, mostly portable or point-of-care instruments checked against laboratory analysis, detect benzodiazepines: in 59 samples, a portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometer identified 36% of those containing etizolam (78% when etizolam was more than 3% of the sample by weight), against 9% with infrared spectroscopy. At one Canadian service, infrared analysis found alprazolam in 33 of 139 samples (23.7%) that people expected to be alprazolam (Xanax), and of 20 sent for confirmatory testing, 14 contained other active ingredients only. In a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group (Park et al., 2020, read in full), among 68 of 103 women who sell or trade sex and use opioids in Baltimore, followed up on average 56 days (not one month, as the review says) after receiving fentanyl test strips with training, counselling and naloxone, reported using alone fell from 95 to 68 in 100 (among the 59 who used opioids at follow-up; the review's 96% is the figure for all 103 at the start) and benzodiazepine use from 22 to 7 in 100; but the baseline drug-use questions covered six months and the follow-up questions one month, the counselling and insert card themselves addressed using alone and mixing other drugs with opioids, the women who used no strip also reduced daily opioid use (9 of 11 to 4 of 11), and overdose, the study's main planned outcome, did not change significantly (6 to 1 women). In an observational study of 541 clients of harm-reduction programmes in three US states, followed for 28 days in 2023 (Gelberg et al., 2025, read in full), a fentanyl test-strip result showing fentanyl, compared with one not showing it, went with more reports of using less, taking turns and keeping naloxone nearby, and the contrast in the amount people reported using was largest when the drugs tested included illicit benzodiazepines (odds ratio 19.9 for reporting less rather than the same or more, against 2.2 for opioids alone); after a result not showing fentanyl on such drugs, using more was reported in a modelled 66 in 100 cases (37 in 100 for opioids alone). The fold reductions that the paper's abstract, and the review's table, give are these odds ratios, not measured falls in the amount used; the study relates self-reported results to self-reported behaviour, measures neither harm nor overdose and does not compare people offered drug checking with people who were not, and the review's text words this association as an effect. Prescribed benzodiazepines were described for 6 of 77 residents of COVID-19 isolation hotels, whose programme as a whole reported no overdoses (an evaluation the review cites as a preprint), and for more than 70 people experiencing homelessness in Dublin, from whom no feedback was collected; in one inner-London general practice, opioid substitution patients maintained on benzodiazepines (127 of 278) stayed in treatment longer than those prescribed none or only briefly (72 months against 34 and 51) and had a lower death rate in treatment than those prescribed none (1.31 against 1.79 per 100 patient-years; the review's table says the occasionally prescribed group had the lowest in-treatment death rate, without a figure), but a larger rise in deaths after leaving treatment, by figures the review reports inconsistently. After Australia moved alprazolam to a stricter schedule in 2014, four of five evaluations summarized in a 2021 review reported large falls in alprazolam use, along with falls in prescribing, dispensing, overdose deaths and poison-centre calls, while figures the authors cite from a letter, without definitions, show benzodiazepine overdose deaths overall rising from 160 in 2009 to 238 in 2015. After the United Kingdom rescheduled temazepam gel capsules, 100 people with long-term use of several drugs, in a qualitative study, described less injecting of capsules but continued injecting of tablets, higher prices, more acquisitive crime and substitution with flunitrazepam. The authors call drug checking the most widely reported approach, with consistently positive outcomes, and the results of prescribing and policy approaches mixed, without having appraised any source; they find harm reduction largely missing for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment, and note that their search, built on the term harm reduction, may have missed studies. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Drug checking, prescribed benzos and stricter rules have all been tried for people who use benzos, but none has been tested in a way that shows whether it lowers harm. The review's authors call drug checking's results consistently positive, but those results are mostly about what tests detected and what people said they did afterwards. At one checking service, infrared testing found alprazolam, the drug in Xanax, in about 1 in 4 samples people thought were Xanax, and some testing methods often missed 'designer' benzos.
population: People who use benzodiazepines (prescribed, diverted, counterfeit or novel), in 35 sources gathered by one scoping review, most of which also involved opioids or stimulants: drug samples at checking services, clients of harm reduction services, women who do sex work, residents of COVID-19 isolation hotels, people in treatment, emergency-department and festival patients, forum posters and poison-centre callers
exposure: Harm reduction services and policies: drug checking, prescribed benzodiazepines (agonist treatment or safer supply), rescheduling, prescribing rules, toxicosurveillance and a poison-centre line
comparator: Mostly none; a few observational comparisons (patients maintained on benzodiazepines against others; positive against negative test results), before-and-after measurements without a control group, and one detection method against another (mostly portable or point-of-care methods against laboratory analysis)
outcome: Detection of benzodiazepines in drug samples; reported behaviour after testing; treatment retention and mortality; prescribing, use and deaths after policy changes; people's accounts
magnitude: No pooled estimates. Detection: portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometry 36% of etizolam-containing samples (78% above 3% by weight) against 9% with infrared (59 samples); a miniature mass spectrometer quantified etizolam in 11 of 15 samples that strips and/or infrared had failed to detect or quantify. Expected alprazolam: 33 of 139 (23.7%) by infrared; of 20 confirmed, 2 alprazolam alone, 4 alprazolam with other ingredients, 14 other ingredients only. Toronto: of 555 samples, 15 were expected to be benzodiazepines, and benzodiazepine-type drugs were found in 116; benzodiazepine-type drugs present in 24 (41%) of samples linked to a negative effect (presence, not cause). After test strips (pilot, 68 of 103 followed up on average 56 days later; Park et al., read in full): using alone 94.9% to 67.8% (n = 59), benzodiazepine use 22.1% to 7.4%, the baseline window six months and the follow-up window one month; daily opioid use among the 11 women who used no strip 81.8% to 36.4%; overdose in the past month 6 to 1 women, not significant; at least one harm reduction behaviour after a positive result 33 of 48 (68.8%). Test-strip results and later behaviour (541 adults, 28 days, observational; Gelberg et al., read in full): odds ratio for reporting less rather than the same or more, positive against negative result, 4.37 (3.45 to 5.55) overall, 19.92 (8.57 to 46.27) for illicit benzodiazepines, 10.04 for stimulants only, 4.21 for opioids and stimulants, 2.18 for opioids only, 2.11 for other or unknown drugs; modelled probability of using more after a negative result 0.657 (benzodiazepines), 0.531 (stimulants only), 0.373 (opioids only), 0.225 overall; after a positive result, overall, less or none 0.090, same 0.847, more 0.063. Prescribed benzodiazepines: 6 of 77 hotel residents (cited from a preprint); more than 70 people in Dublin. Opioid substitution case notes: retention 72 against 34 and 51 months; in-treatment mortality 1.31 against 1.79 per 100 patient-years (against those prescribed none; lowest in the occasionally prescribed group, no figure given); post-treatment rate in the maintained group 5.90 per 100 years, reported as a 450% rise (4.5 times the in-treatment rate, an increase of about 350%, editors' calculation). Alprazolam rescheduling: 4 of 5 evaluations reported large declines in use; alprazolam-related deaths 57 (2012) to 23 (2015); benzodiazepine overdose deaths 160 (2009) to 238 (2015). Kentucky 'no benzodiazepine' formulary: prescriptions down 89% over two years. Victoria emergency departments, 2020 to 2022: novel benzodiazepine-type drugs in 183 of 1112 drug-toxicity presentations (16.5%). Poison-centre line: safety information to 6635 of 17,616 callers (37.7%), no outcome evaluation.

risk_of_bias.note: The review appraised none of its sources (two of them, the test-strip pilot and cohort, have since been read in full: ROBINS-I critical and serious); designs are pilot, cross-sectional, qualitative, uncontrolled before-and-after or descriptive; the review attributes programme-wide outcomes to benzodiazepine prescribing, and its counts contain errors (card sc_morrison_2025); the isolation-hotel evaluation is cited from a preprint.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: different approaches, not repeated tests of one approach.

indirectness.note: Second-hand, and some figures third-hand (a 2021 review and a letter cited by the authors); detection accuracy stands in for outcomes that matter to people; most people and samples involved opioids and other drugs as well.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed; grey and peer-led literature were not searched.

grade.reasoning: Observational and descriptive sources start low; rated down for risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low. The claim rests only on a scoping review, a narrative synthesis without appraisal (designed as a narrative review on its card), so it stays at draft and its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3). Insufficient evidence: no approach was evaluated against a comparison able to show an effect on harm; the only comparisons are observational (one practice's case notes; test-strip results related to later reported behaviour, an outcome of behaviour, not harm) or before-and-after without a control group, and the authors' more favourable reading of drug checking rests on detection studies and reported behaviour. Status single study: the claim rests on one review, and no approach has two controlled evaluations. Two primary sources have now been read in full (round pdf-2026-11-01): the test-strip pilot (Park et al., 2020) and the test-strip cohort (Gelberg et al., 2025); they correct the review's account (follow-up on average 56 days, not one month; a six-month baseline window against one month at follow-up; fold reductions that are odds ratios) and add that, when benzodiazepines were tested, a result without fentanyl was often followed by reports of using more. They are cited as qualifiers, so the claim still rests on the scoping review for its main finding and stays at draft with its other figures second-hand. The other primary sources (for example the alprazolam test results and the London case notes) have not been read.
